When to Build a New Project
Not every request needs a full project build. Use this to decide when the pipeline is the right move and when a simpler approach will do.
Build a project when...
  • A workflow recurs often enough that multiple people would use it
  • The task requires School Tech-specific context to answer well
  • You want consistent, reliable behavior across users
  • The output quality matters and needs to be validated
  • You want the tool to be maintainable and improvable over time
  • The request is role-specific (support, SF admin, etc.)
Don't build a project when...
  • It is a one-off task that will not be repeated
  • A quick chat with AI Advisor already handles it
  • The scope is unclear - scope it first, then build
  • Only one person will ever use it and infrequently
  • The workflow is still changing and not stable yet
  • You only need a quick prompt - use The Architect's Quick Prompt mode instead
If you are not sure: Start a conversation in AI Advisor and try to accomplish the task manually. If you find yourself wishing the tool had specific context or behaved differently on repeated use, that is a signal to build a project.
Before You Build: The Core Brain
Every project you build draws from a shared pool of foundational company knowledge - the "core brain." These are context files that live in context-files/shared/ and get uploaded to any project that needs them. Building the core brain once means every future project starts with accurate, consistent company context instead of rediscovering it from scratch each time.
Do this before building your first real project. Without the core brain files, every agent you build will either lack company context or contain inconsistent one-off descriptions of STA's products, team, and customers. Work the two steps below in order; there is no separate checklist file to open.
Historical - 2026-04-29 plan, retained for context (noted 2026-08-19). The seven files below were the planned core-brain set as of 2026-04-29. Several shipped under different names and the planned filenames here do not match the live shared-context set, so do not treat this table as a current inventory or use these filenames when building. The live shared context files are the authority - read them from the registry and from the Projects that carry them. The method still holds: seed one file, then produce the rest by running Deep Research and distilling the output via the knowledge-base-context-builder skill.

How to produce the core brain files
Deep Research + KB Context Builder

Step 1 - Run Deep Research. Ask Deep Research for a full public-source profile of STA. Deep Research hits all public-facing sources for STA - website, LinkedIn, industry databases, conference mentions, press - and saves structured modules to Knowledge Base/sta/sta-company-profile/. This fills the web-researchable portion of every file above.

Step 2 - Fill internal gaps. For the files marked "needs internal input" in the table above (team responsibilities, full customer list, ICP, partnership terms), gather that information directly from the relevant team member. Add it to the Deep Research modules or capture it as notes for Step 3.

Step 3 - Distill into context-shared files. Open The Architect and run the knowledge-base-context-builder skill, pointing it at the Deep Research output modules. It formats them into clean, upload-ready context files and saves them to context-files/shared/. The 7 files in the table above are the target outputs.

Step 4 - Upload to projects. Any Claude.ai Project that needs company context gets the relevant context-shared file(s) uploaded. Cowork projects read them directly from the workspace - no upload needed. When a file is updated, re-upload it to any Claude.ai Projects that use it.

Context-shared vs. project-specific: Files in context-files/shared/ are foundational - used across multiple projects. Files in Project Blueprints/[name]/ are project-specific (tone references, escalation paths, product-specific rules). When in doubt, put it in context-shared if more than one future project would need it.

Registry + Files
All pipeline tools are in Cowork. The Architect is a Cowork project. Run Test Cases and Project Feedback are Cowork skills (auto-loaded by trigger phrases). All admin-only - regular staff do not have access.
Step 1 - Build with The Architect
1
Discovery, blueprint, instructions, test cases, registry entry, handoff - all in one session
The Architect

Open the The Architect Cowork project. Describe the workflow you want to automate. The Architect runs through four phases (Discovery, KB Check, Gap Analysis, Blueprint) and produces production-ready files - not scaffolds. Output is split into two waves with a confirmation gate between them.

Starting prompt format:
I want to build a new project for [role/team]. The workflow is: [describe what the user would ask and what a good response looks like]. Deployment target: [Cowork / Claude.ai Project / Both].
Wave 1 - the prompt wave (produced first)
The Architect saves blueprint-summary.md, instructions.md, any context files needed, and backlog.md (a lightweight tracker for future enhancement ideas, with Active and Implemented sections). Production-ready, not a draft. While iterating, you can ask The Architect to run the prompt-evaluator skill on instructions.md - it returns a scored HTML eval saved as a real .html file (not a Cowork artifact) under The Architect/prompt-evaluation/[Project Name]/[Project Name] v[X.Y].html, one folder per project/Cowork and one file per version (per the v6.16 eval-output rule).
⏸ Confirmation gate
After Wave 1 saves, The Architect asks: "Is the instructions.md final, or do you want changes?" Iterate on the prompt until you explicitly say it is final. Wave 2 is held until that confirmation - this is the v3.0 timing rule, designed to prevent rework when the prompt changes.
Wave 2 - downstream files (produced after confirmation)
The Architect saves test-cases.md (10 full test cases, not a scaffold), registry-entry.md (the row to add to context-agent-registry.md plus scope-overlap notes), project-launch.md (three copy-paste blocks: project instructions ready to paste into project settings, a numbered setup checklist of every manual step, and an initialization prompt to send as the first message to verify setup), and handoff.md (pipeline tracker).
All saved to C:\Users\Adam\Documents\Claude\Project Blueprints\[project-name]/
blueprint-summary.md instructions.md (production-ready) backlog.md test-cases.md registry-entry.md project-launch.md handoff.md
The Architect's five modes: Full Pipeline (new project from scratch - default). Polish Existing (you provide an existing prompt to bring up to standard; The Architect verifies via filesystem check that no live blueprint folder exists before treating as Polish). Quick Prompt (lightweight one-off, no pipeline tracking, no registry). Test Case Update (revise test-cases.md after any change to instructions - Project Feedback fix, manual edit, polish revision, eval-driven update). Advisory (expert Q&A - opinions, assessments, recommendations; KB-grounded answers, no pipeline artifacts, no registry). The Architect picks the mode based on your opening message and confirms it back ("I'm reading this as [Mode] because [signal]. Sound right?") before running the workflow. If the opening is ambiguous, it surfaces both candidate modes and asks which applies. Quick Prompt and Advisory skip the confirmation when intent is unambiguous.
Phase loopback: Phases run in sequence, but if a later phase reveals a miss in an earlier phase (e.g., Phase 4 needs a constraint that wasn't asked about in Discovery), The Architect returns to that phase rather than barreling forward. Single-sentence pause: "I'm at [phase] and just realized I never asked [question]. Going back to [earlier phase] for one question."
Step 2 - Deploy the Project
2
Create the workspace or project and paste the instructions
Cowork or Claude.ai

Where you deploy depends on who the audience is. Cowork is for internal admin tools and pipeline tools. Claude.ai Projects are for team-facing tools that all staff access.

Target Use When How to Deploy
Cowork Admin-only tool, pipeline tool, work personal assistant Open Cowork - New Project - paste name and instructions. Upload context files if required.
Claude.ai Team-facing tool, staff-accessible workflow claude.ai - Projects - New Project - paste instructions. Add context files. Share with team members.
Both Tool used by both admins and regular staff The Architect produces two instructions files (instructions-cowork.md and instructions-project.md) plus a single shared changelog. Deploy each to its target. Keep both versions in sync via the changelog.

After deploying, do not set Status to Active in the registry yet - that happens in Step 5 after Run Test Cases confirms tests pass.

Step 3 - Test with Run Test Cases
3
Run the 10 test cases and get a pass/fail report
Run Test Cases

Open The Architect (or any Cowork session with the run-test-cases skill enabled) and trigger Run Test Cases by saying "test my project." Point it at the blueprint folder. It reads instructions.md and test-cases.md, runs all 10 cases (batch or walkthrough mode), and produces a report with pass/fail results and specific failure details.

Exact prompt:
Test my project. The blueprint is at Project Blueprints/[project-name]/. Run all 10 test cases in batch mode and give me a full pass/fail report. Save the report as Project Blueprints/[project-name]/test-report-[today's date].md

A pass rate of 8/10 or higher is the target before going live with a team-facing tool. For admin-only tools, 7/10 is acceptable if the failures are edge cases.

Run Test Cases checks the v3.0 timing rule automatically: if test-cases.md and instructions.md were produced against different versions, it flags the mismatch before running.

Saved to Project Blueprints/[project-name]/
test-report-[date].md
Step 4 - Fix Issues with Project Feedback
4
Turn test failures or live-use bugs into exact-text instruction fixes
Project Feedback

For each failure in the test report (or each issue spotted in live use), trigger the Project Feedback skill. Describe what went wrong. Project Feedback reads the current instructions, identifies the root cause (Missing instruction / Wrong instruction / Conflicting instructions / Scope gap / Overly broad instruction), and produces the exact text to add, change, or remove.

Prompt format:
Fix my project. Blueprint at Project Blueprints/[project-name]/. Issue: [paste the failure or describe the bad behavior]. The correct behavior should be: [describe what should have happened].

After applying the fix, re-paste the updated instructions into the deployed workspace or project. Increment the version in the instructions.md changelog and in handoff.md (v1.0 - v1.1 - etc.).

If the fix changes test coverage, take the updated instructions back to The Architect and ask it to run the Test Case Update workflow. The Architect compares the changelog entry to the existing test cases and produces a revised test-cases.md with [UPDATED] and [NEW] markers. Re-run Run Test Cases after.

Repeat until you hit your target pass rate.

Step 5 - Lock It In
5
Update registry and finalize handoff
Registry + Files

Once the project passes testing, do the following in order:

1. Apply the registry entry. Open The Architect/context-agent-registry.md and append (or update) the row from Project Blueprints/[project-name]/registry-entry.md. Status moves from Draft to Active here.

2. Finalize handoff.md. Confirm Status = Active, Current Version matches the deployed version, Testing row reflects the run-test-cases report, and all open USER TO PROVIDE markers are resolved.

3. Update AI System Overview Admin.html if the new project changes anything about how the system works or introduces a new tool type.

4. If the project has a knowledge base dependency, confirm the relevant module exists in Knowledge Base/index.md and that the context file uploaded to the project is current.

Backup note: The workspace folder is backed up to GitHub on a weekly schedule. No manual step required, and nothing needs to be left open for it to run - but the cadence is weekly, so recent work is not necessarily captured yet. Repo: github.com/abaker421/school-tech-ai-system (private).
Standing deliverable: case study. Every project (and every training course) gets a case study HTML file saved to Training Materials/Training - Admin/[project-slug]-case-study.html. After Step 5, ask The Architect to build the case study. Before it starts, The Architect will ask which specific real session or build to use as the live walkthrough example - it will suggest 1-3 known candidates in the same message. Confirm the case, then it writes the full file. Add the completed case study to the hub card index in STA-Training-Hub.html (window.TRAINING_DATA.docs plus the relevant AI Admin section), then sync dist/index.html.
What Gets Saved Where
Every project produces a set of files. This table shows where each one lives, what it is for, and when it gets updated.
File Location Purpose Updated When
blueprint-summary.md Project Blueprints/[name]/ Plain-language scope, audience, design decisions, open USER TO PROVIDE markers, tool assessment At project creation - rarely after
instructions.md Project Blueprints/[name]/ Production-ready system prompt with version changelog. Source of truth for what is pasted into the live workspace. Every time Project Feedback or The Architect produces a change. Always increments version.
test-cases.md Project Blueprints/[name]/ 10 complete test cases (3 normal use, 2 ambiguous, 2 uncertainty, 2 edge case, 1 output format) Produced after instructions.md is confirmed final. Updated by The Architect's Test Case Update mode after fixes.
registry-entry.md Project Blueprints/[name]/ The canonical row for context-agent-registry.md plus scope-overlap notes At project creation. Updated if registry layout changes.
handoff.md Project Blueprints/[name]/ Pipeline tracker - which stages are complete, current version, deployment target, notes Every time a stage transitions (testing complete, version increments, etc.)
test-report-[date].md Project Blueprints/[name]/ Most recent Run Test Cases run results After each Run Test Cases run (supersedes prior reports)
context-tone-reference.md Project Blueprints/[name]/ Tone and style reference for the project (optional) Created if the project has tone-sensitive output. Upload as context to the live project.
context-agent-registry.md The Architect/ (workspace root) Master list of all projects - used by The Architect to check for scope overlap When a project is added, deprecated, or significantly changed
[Project Name] v[X.Y].html The Architect/prompt-evaluation/[Project Name]/ (one folder per project/Cowork) Optional prompt-evaluator score report. v6.16+ saves a real .html file per evaluated version (the folder is the persistent history); not a Cowork artifact. Run during Step 1 iteration if useful for grading the prompt before confirming final.
Common Pitfalls
Producing Wave 2 files before instructions.md is confirmed final
If you skip the v3.0 confirmation gate, every prompt change after invalidates the test cases and forces a rewrite. The Architect holds Wave 2 by design - don't push it through prematurely.
Deploying before testing
Skipping Run Test Cases because "it seems fine" is how tools end up with subtle but consistent failures that erode user trust. Always run at least a batch test before going live with a team-facing project.
Not updating instructions.md after a fix
When Project Feedback produces a fix and you paste it into the workspace, you must also update instructions.md in the blueprint folder. If you only update the live workspace, the file and the deployed version drift apart. The next maintenance cycle will re-introduce the bug.
Skipping the Test Case Update workflow after a fix
When Project Feedback fixes a bug, the existing test cases may not cover the new behavior. Take the updated instructions back to The Architect and run Test Case Update mode - it produces a revised test-cases.md with [UPDATED] and [NEW] markers. Then re-run Run Test Cases. Don't rely on the old test cases.
Forgetting the registry
If a new project is not added to context-agent-registry.md, The Architect cannot check for scope overlap when building the next project. Over time the registry becomes stale and overlap detection stops working.
